contributions: Practical literary interpretation, narrative form, close reading and critical sources directly implement the literary-analysis discipline; no French corpus is implied.

International-relations theories, historical/colonial cases and country-position research provide a specific institutional/geopolitical context for France and international-organisation interests; a French country project is not guaranteed.

Comparative close reading of literary works and recurring themes supplies sustained literary study without claiming a French-language canon.
Actual language acquisition, bilingualism and comprehension/production inquiry directly support the multilingual-language element; no French-specific linguistic sequence is claimed.
Modern nationalism, ideologies, industrialisation and world wars provide specific historical context for interpreting modern European cultural questions, without a French-specialist sequence.
Film form, expressionism, adaptation and independent interpretation provide concrete film/media analytical methods; not a complete French film-history sequence.
Print, optical and sound media as cultural artifacts supply material-historical methods for studying mediated culture, not specifically French media content.
Classical theories including Marx and Weber, modernity and stratification supply specific social-theoretical tools for interpreting culture and historical change.
Interviews, textual/documentary and visual analysis, coding, reflexivity and research ethics provide concrete empirical humanities/cultural-research complements.
Life narratives, memory, identity and cultural positioning are analysed through close reading and comparative research; it is not a French study-abroad replacement.
Philosophical arguments about mind, identity, experience and mind–body relations complement the explicit language/brain and reflective humanities inquiry.
Documentary analysis, historical/ethical representation, interviewing and short-film research develop concrete cultural analysis and research practice.
Adaptation theory, medium specificity, intertextuality and text/film research directly extend literary and cultural interpretation.
Comparative myth, narrative transmission and literary theory provide a comparative literary contribution, not French myth/corpus teaching.
Actual European institutions, integration and policy-document research provide a specific complement to the evidenced France/Europe question; no French political history course is invented.
Critical theory, modernity, phenomenology and cultural/social interpretation provide specific theoretical perspectives for interpreting cultural identity and power.
Actual ethical arguments and close reading provide philosophical inquiry; this is not equated with the external Philosophy of Culture syllabus.
Humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic interpretation is applied in literary research, directly sustaining the humanities core.
Poetic form, sound, voice, performance and research-grounded creative work directly supply literary/communicative inquiry; no French-language creative-writing equivalence.
